newsitem.title: GHANA: Ashanti looks to improve as 100th birthday nears.
newsitem.headline: Ashanti looks to improve as 100th birthday nears.

text.p: West African mining giant Ashanti Goldfields Co Ltd celebrates its 100th birthday on Wednesday and is pinning hopes on improving its performance with two mines set to open next year.
Ashanti says it will postpone centennial celebrations to coincide with the opening of the two new mines in 1998, including one near its first site at Obuasi, southwest Ghana.
Ashanti produced gold at Obuasi in December 1897 after making its London Stock Exchange debut on June 11 that year.

Profits at Ashanti have declined in recent years. It pins hopes of a turnaround in part on its 170,000 ounces/year mine at Bibiani -- 80 km west of its Obuasi mine. It is due on line in 1998 along with a new 160,000 ounces/year mine at Siguiri in north-east Guinea.
"These new projects will become mines in the coming year at which time there will be a cause for some celebration to mark our centenary," said Anaman.

"We are proud of achievements made in 100 years in Ghana. We emerged in recent years as a leading Panafrican mining company with presence in 12 African countries, working on 35 projects," corporate affairs manager, James Anaman, told Reuters.
After being swallowed by international conglomerate Lonrho, Ashanti's name returned to the London Stock Exchange as an independent company in 1994 with Lonrho retaining a stake.
Analysts, including French bankers Paribas, say there is no reason for immediate jubilation as Ashanti is just beginning to pick up again.
"The company has suffered considerably over the past couple of years as costs escalated out of control," wrote Banque Paribas analysts in January in a wide-ranging report.
With the start of Ashanti's operational independence from Lonrho in 1994, the company did not succeed in controlling costs, the report said.

Ashanti's 1996 annual report puts 1995 operating costs at $213.6 million, or $177 per ounce, against $146.3 million, or $227 per ounce, in 1994. Costs in 1996 crept up to $280.7 million, or $271 per ounce.
Analysts now expect net 1998 profits to rise by $26 million to $81.7 million. In 1995, net profits stood at $110.6 million.
"Ashanti is on track to meet production and cost forecasts in 1997," said another analyst in a Banque Bruxelles Lambert France report.
Ashanti is targeting an annualised gold production rate of over 1.1 milion ounces with cash operating cost kept below $265 per ounce.

The company's new mine plans follow a century of output growth from 2,544 ounces of gold produced between March 1898 and June 1899. By 1999, production from Ashanti mines is expected to be around 1.37 million ounces of gold, with at least 850,000 ounces from the Obuasi complex.

Obuasi itself has grown from a single mine to a complex that includes underground and vast open pit mines, heap-leach gold recovery facilities, four treatment plants, and the world's largest bio-oxidation plant.
With total reserves and a resource base of around 21.6 million ounces of gold, Obuasi is set to remain Ashanti's kingpin mine into Ashanti's second century.
